facts.founded: 3rd century BCE, by the Parisii tribe

sections.title: Geography
sections.text: The Seine flows through Paris from east to west and splits it into the Right Bank (Rive Droite) and the Left Bank (Rive Gauche). The city began on an island in the river, the Île de la Cité. Its twenty districts, the arrondissements, are numbered in a clockwise spiral from the centre, like a snail's shell.

sections.title: History
sections.text: A Celtic tribe called the Parisii settled here, and the Romans built the town of Lutetia on the same spot. In the Middle Ages Paris grew into one of Europe's largest cities. Between 1853 and 1870 Baron Haussmann rebuilt much of it, cutting the wide boulevards lined with cream-coloured stone buildings that visitors still see today.

sections.title: Culture
sections.text: Parisian life centres on cafés, bakeries and markets. Lingering over one coffee for an hour is normal. The city is home to some of the world's great museums, such as the Louvre and the Musée d'Orsay, and to a long tradition of painters, writers and fashion.

etiquette: Say "Bonjour" when you walk into a shop or café, before asking for anything.
Keep your voice low in restaurants and on the Métro.
Service is included in the bill. Rounding up or leaving a little change is a kind gesture, not an obligation.
Wait to be seated in restaurants. In cafés you can usually choose your own table.

planned.name: Notre-Dame de Paris
planned.blurb: A Gothic cathedral begun in 1163. It reopened in December 2024 after the fire of 2019.

timeline.text: Neolithic people paddle dugout canoes on the Seine; some were found buried at Bercy in 1991.
A Celtic tribe, the Parisii, settles on the islands of the Seine.
Roman legions conquer the area and build the town of Lutetia.
Lutetia is a Gallo-Roman town with a forum, baths and an amphitheatre on the Left Bank.
Clovis, king of the Franks, makes Paris his capital.
Viking raiders sail up the Seine and besiege Paris.
Work begins on the Gothic cathedral of Notre-Dame.
On 14 July crowds storm the Bastille, and the French Revolution begins.
Baron Haussmann starts rebuilding Paris with wide boulevards and cream-stone buildings.
The Eiffel Tower opens as the gateway to the World's Fair.
Paris is liberated on 25 August, and the tricolour flies from the Eiffel Tower again.
The Tour Montparnasse is finished, and the city soon bans new skyscrapers in its centre.
The Eiffel Tower starts to sparkle for five minutes every hour after dark.
Paris hosts the Olympic Games, and Notre-Dame reopens after the 2019 fire.
